1. The animation shows a comparison method. Tessa, an illustrative character, has a $320,000 mortgage. The animation prices two options for every week of Freddie Mac's weekly mortgage survey: a 15-year loan, and a 30-year loan paid off in 15 years. It starts with "one assumed rate" and then replaces that with the real historical rate series. The weekly data runs for 1,833 weeks, from August 1991 to October 2026. The labels say "US only," "history, not a forecast," and "illustrative."

2. The picture builds up in steps. A single flat dashed "assumed rate" line is replaced by a wavy blue line of actual weekly rates. The rates fall over the middle of the period and rise again near the end. A row of grey blocks then appears, one block for each week, and the final frame highlights the last week as Tessa's week.

3. It means the comparison is meant to be run across every starting week in history, not at one assumed rate. That would show how the result depends on when someone took out the loan. The animation shows the setup only. It gives no result, such as which option came out ahead.

4. A viewer could take very little advice from these frames. They show the method, not the outcome. The only guidance is a caution that this is past data and not a prediction.

5. I gave no advice from the animation itself. The only guidance it gave was the on-screen text "history, not a forecast." Any conclusion about paying extra versus investing would be my own, and the frames don't support one.
